title: Kurt Vile - Breaking and Entering
summary: Kurt Vile talks about his 7th record 'Bottle It In', his love of melancholic music, Obama, and getting lost in hypnotic grooves.
transcript:
Philadelphian singer-songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and producer Kurt Vile visited Triple R during his 2019 Australian tour to discuss his seventh album, Bottle It In. The conversation ranges from home recording and melancholy to Barack Obama, repetition and his collaborations with Courtney Barnett and Kim Gordon. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: Kurt Vile came into Triple R yesterday in the middle of a busy Australian tour. He played the Forum last night with RVG and Boogie on the weekend. I think he was the very last performer, bringing the festival to a close with an hour and a half set. His most recent album, Bottle It In, was foremost on the mind when I started the conversation.

Around the time of its release, Kurt was talking about how the record represents his twin impulses: always trying to get back to his roots, also trying to move forward, and finding a balance between the two. Over his prolific career, he's spoken openly of influences such as Pavement, Neil Young, Tom Petty and John Fahey, but he's also an influential figure who has inspired new generations of songwriters. He's collaborated extensively, working with Courtney Barnett on Lotta Sea Lice, released a year ago or so, and performed as a touring musician with the War on Drugs.

He travels extensively and has also settled into a new residence in Philadelphia, where he lives with his family on the border of an urban area and the woods. Speaking about those impulses of moving forward and reflecting on the past, I asked him where along that spectrum he finds himself at the moment.

Kurt: Even now, I feel like I'm trying to get a homespun thing together again back at home, in my basement, in my KV world. I'm trying to get my KV world back together. My drummer even said, once you reach 40 you start looking back at your whole life. I'm not 40 yet, I'm 39, but I kind of like looking back. I like the idea of going through old recordings or going back to old methods, and taking them forward at the same time.

I used to just record on this little digital Roland eight-track and put all kinds of cheap effects on it because otherwise it would sound like clean digital straight into the machine. Times have changed since then, since the early 2000s or whatever it was. A lot of people I know are masters of recording on the computer, but I still am not that. I get reel-to-reel tape machines, microphones and all kinds of gear. Slowly but surely, with the help of friends, I'm getting my world together, and I decided to keep it pretty analogue for now. Throw the computer out the window, because once you open the screen there's a million things going on, just like the phone screen. I'm definitely trying to listen to cassette tapes and record on reel-to-reel tape when I can, and figure out the rest later. At least I'm focusing on the music.

Simon: Technology and how it's affecting us is a huge conversation, and you reflect on that directly in some of the lyrics on this album. You've said in the past that your favourite songs are often the most melancholic. Why are you drawn naturally to melancholy?

Kurt: I think it's true, probably, that the most beautiful things come out of a place of struggle and sadness or whatever. But even when I'm happy, I always think life is bittersweet and beautiful. I've got kids and they're awesome. It's awesome to embrace what's beautiful in the moment, but there's plenty of things to distract you.

We're also very lucky people. I'm a lucky person, and there's plenty of people who are not even close to as lucky as we are. There's just bizarre things going on. I guess we're hypersensitive to it now because it all goes to our phones. But also, it's a pretty cartoon, ridiculous world right now, like America's president or whatever, et cetera. It's like they're intentionally trying to daze you as well, and it worked. I'm done talking about it.

Simon: That's fair enough. I hope you don't mind a little segue, but talking about American politics, a former president, Barack Obama, nominated one of your songs as one of his favourites.

Kurt: That was amazing. 'One Trick Ponies'. My wife, Suzanne, she worships both Obama and his wife, Michelle. I think he's amazing too. He's just one of those people who emits this positivity. Obviously he's just a positive person, and that'd be amazing to meet him. Who knows?

Simon: It'd be nice if he had a podcast, hey.

Simon: It was lovely to have your song isolated by him, potentially bringing it to new audiences. What's your relationship with 'One Trick Ponies' in the context of the album?

Kurt: That was my idea of the pop song, and I did it with Rob Schnapf, who I first worked with on the last record. The first song we did with him was 'Pretty Pimpin', and that was definitely my most successful song. I guess I had similar ideas for this song being a pop jam. It's a little longer, more verses. It's just saying all the people in my life that I love, some I don't talk to, some are not around any more. But the true ones, it's like you have a best friend, or one of your best friends, you could not talk to him for years and then see him tomorrow, and it's just like you saw him yesterday.

Simon: It's a remarkable achievement as a songwriter to capture the sweep of someone's life in lyrics which last for less than six minutes. You find that balance beautifully.

Kurt: It's funny, we haven't been able to get this song together live yet. Granted, I don't give people that much of a chance, I give them a 30-second window. Part of it is those harmonies. Stella Mozgawa from Warpaint, I love collaborating with her, and then Farmer Dave Scher, two California types, basically. Well, Stella's from Sydney actually. But that's a very West Coast thing, working over there with them, and I bring it to the Violators, who are very East Coast. I know we'll get there eventually, but basically I've only given them about 20 seconds to get it, and we haven't gotten it yet.

Simon: Kurt Vile was also acclaimed for his participation in the War on Drugs, where he was the lead guitarist. His debut album, Constant Hitmaker, was self-released in 2008. He signed to Matador Records in 2009, releasing his third album and debut for the label, Childish Prodigy. In this next section we go deeper into revisiting and returning in life and music, and getting lost in a groove: the hypnosis he found in 'Bottle It In', his favourite on the album.

Kurt: Basically, the backbone of the song is these warbly keyboard things, and I had the lyrics. The morning before I left, I just recorded it in my house. I stayed up all night and recorded it, and I was like, okay, here's the basic song, it's 11 minutes long, we'll cut it down later. Sure enough, I didn't have time to cut it down, so Stella showed up and she just jammed to it while I sang live to her, because that's a true reaction. I was just trying to get things as musical as possible. I sang along my lyrics and I was like, okay, we'll cut this down later. But then the whole thing was sort of like a spiritual jazz, hypnotic song, minimal orchestral hypnotic type of tune.

My friend Mary Lattimore added harp to it, which is basically the only melodic thing in there. In the middle there's a horn solo played on a Mellotron. I was singing, then I took a break and played that in the moment. Those are the kind of little tricks I've learned along the way. I'm going to sing, but make sure I have a guitar on my neck just in case, or turn that keyboard on. Have as many people play live as possible. Let's get this thing over with, and then it usually comes off more organic and natural that way anyway.

Simon: 'One Trick Ponies' has the memorable line, which seems to relate to hypnosis and hypnotic grooves, that you've always had a soft spot for repetition.

Kurt: Totally. Definitely in music, which some people who don't favour this record try to use against me, but that's fine. Also repetition in comedy, saying the same jokes over and over again with the same inflections, saying things the same exact way over and over again. So it either becomes a little funnier every time or a little more annoying every time. Either one is rewarding to me. If I make somebody laugh a little harder every time, or if I annoy them a little more every time, those are both rewarding to me. It's a success.

Simon: To stay a little longer on getting locked into a groove, a musician whom you deeply admire is Neil Young. There's a great story about when you met Neil backstage, talking about taking people places in their music. He said to you, 'We can go into outer space whenever we want.'

Kurt: That's what he said. That was amazing. I basically was just saying, 'I saw you 10 times. It's the best by far.' 'Down by the River' sounded like you were underground. It was very organic, but in outer space, because he was really messing with the audience. It was like a 30-minute-long 'Down by the River'. You'd think he was going into the last verse after a space jam, and then he would just say, 'Be on my side,' and go back into playing. You'd think it was the last verse, but he would just say that one line and go back into outer space. I was like, 'It was like you're in outer space.' 'Oh yeah, we can go to outer space whenever we want.'

It's funny, that's just true to him. I've read all his bios or whatever, Shakey I guess is the main one, which I'm sure he doesn't love. Who loves a book about them? But still, they get those long monologues of him just ranting, and he's just so confident, rightly so. I learn a lot from that. I'll play that card. Next fan comes up to me, I'll try to play that same card.

Simon: That's a great card. I think about it in relation to your new album as well, the hypnosis, the grooves and the transportative quality of the music. Maybe that's a line you reflect on when you're writing or performing, this idea of transporting people into these outer worlds.

Kurt: Yeah, I mean, I can also go to outer space whenever I want.

Simon: Exactly. That's what I wanted you to say.

Kurt: But it's true.

Simon: Collaboration is a big part of your work. We loved Lotta Sea Lice with Courtney Barnett, and I think it was an Album of the Week here.

Kurt: That's my girl. That's my sis from the other side.

Simon: There are collaborations on your solo records, such as Kim Gordon and Cass McCombs on this album. I understand Kim Gordon is a big fan from Childish Prodigy days.

Kurt: She was really into that album, which was very surreal, because I had just signed to Matador. The first of my childhood heroes to really acknowledge me, I guess, was Dinosaur Jr. He said it was his favourite album of the year, or one of them, on an end-of-the-year list. Then he invited us on tour, and I was like, oh, here we go.

At the first show or something, someone was like, 'Kim Gordon's at the merch table.' Of course we didn't have anybody, and I just ran over there. She was looking at my merch, and she's like, 'Oh, I love Childish Prodigy.' I remember I had stalked Thurston, they were still together. I had randomly given him CD-Rs in my life, so he was aware of me. But then Thurston was like, 'When Kim gets into something, she really gets into something.' I think she sort of hijacked me and made it her own, and that was fine with me. Apparently she would just listen to it all the time.

Simon: I don't know if this is true or not, but apparently she threatened the producer of your next album not to mess it up.

Kurt: She was busting his balls. But all those things happened at once. Around that same time, I met John Agnello, who had worked with Dinosaur Jr and Sonic Youth on their last records, and this was not lost on me. I knew I was going to work with John Agnello. I wanted to be in that world. Even on Childish Prodigy I covered Dim Stars, which is Thurston Moore and Steve Shelley and Richard Hell. There's a song called 'Monkey' that they did. So it wasn't lost that I might go down that rabbit hole if I'm lucky.

While I was in the studio she was like, 'We heard you're working on the next Kurt Vile. Man, I love Childish Prodigy so much. Better not screw it up.'

Simon: Exactly. The pressure's on.
